title: Our heart is restless (Confessions 1.1)
hookLine: the pull that keeps you refreshing an empty feed: Augustine opens his book on it
tomorrow: how do you invite in someone who already fills the house?
last: WITH ESTEEM · THE COURTYARD · UNITY, NOT SAMENESS.

cards: Late at night, your thumb refreshes a feed with nothing new in it. Then another app. Then the fridge, then back.
Nothing's wrong, exactly. Nobody needs you. Something just won't settle.
Yesterday's question was what Augustine actually wrote first. Not his birthplace. Not his sins.
His first words are spoken to God, in Pusey's translation: "Great art Thou, O Lord, and greatly to be praised." And a few lines later, the sentence about that thumb.

teach.b: Here it is: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." Three pieces. Thou madest us for Thyself: before a word about sin or searching, Augustine starts with what people are for.
Our heart is restless: not my heart.
He doesn't keep the restlessness as his private flaw; he puts it in the plural, for everyone listening in. Until it repose in Thee: the restlessness has a direction.
It isn't only a problem to fix; it's a pull toward something. His Latin word is inquietum, unquiet.
And around the line, he asks a question that sounds backward: should a person call on God first, or know him first? He doesn't settle it neatly.
He leans on a promise instead: those who seek the Lord will find him, and those who find him will praise him. So he reaches, and praises while he reaches.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes this very page where it describes the desire for God, the longing it says is written in the human heart.
That's the shape of the whole Confessions: a restless man telling his life back to the one he was restless for.

how: The Catechism quotes this opening of the Confessions in its section on the desire for God, and some Catholics read the Confessions slowly as spiritual reading, a few paragraphs at a time.

games.q: what does “our heart is restless” mean?
o: a heart troubled by worry over money and work
a heart broken by a grief that won't quite heal
a heart made for God, unquiet until it rests in him

games.q: the first page — tap the pairs.
p: a life told back to God

s: the Confessions opens with Augustine's birthplace
it opens by speaking to God: great art Thou, O Lord.
in this line, restlessness is just stress to get rid of
it has a direction: until it repose in Thee. it's a pull, not only a problem.
Augustine writes our heart, not my heart
he puts the restlessness in the plural, for everyone listening in.

games.q: your friend just got everything she wanted this year, the team, the grades, the plans, and says she still feels oddly unsettled. what would Augustine's first page say?
o: that feeling has a direction: the heart was made for more than a list.
she's stressed and should take a few days off to recover.
she must have done something wrong, and the feeling is guilt.
games.why: Confessions 1.1 treats restlessness as a pull toward God, not only a symptom: our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper and write down, in two or three words, the restlessness in you right now: an urge to check something, a want you can't quite name.
Don't fix it or scold it; just let it sit on the paper while you rest. If you pray, you can hold that word up to God the way Augustine held his, as a direction and not only a problem.

wordCard.voice: Our heart is restless. Augustine's line from his first page: made for God, and unquiet until we rest in him.

orig.note: Latin, Confessions 1.1: our heart is restless, unquiet, until it rests in God.

carryVoice: Keep this one: restless until. The sentence doesn't stop at restless; it keeps going, toward rest. Good night, restless heart.
